claims.text: Uniform atomic mixing in near-equiatomic, multi-element nanoparticles kinetically slows atomic diffusion at high temperatures.
Configurational-entropy stabilization inhibits phase separation in high-entropy solid solutions.
Uniform atomic mixing prevents segregation of noble-metal components during high-temperature service.
Sustained structural homogeneity preserves chemical and catalytic performance under service conditions.
One-pot colloidal or solvothermal synthesis yields near-equiatomic, uniformly atomically mixed high-entropy alloy or oxide nanoparticles.
Stepwise reduction or sequential metal addition can deliberately produce controlled partial compositional inhomogeneity.
Lattice strain and uniform elemental distributions measured by high-resolution TEM and elemental mapping indicate atomic mixing and solid-solution integrity.
High configurational entropy creates high kinetic barriers for atomic diffusion.
Atomic-size differences produce lattice distortion that lowers atomic diffusivity in high-entropy alloys.
Partial compositional inhomogeneity permits faster local atomic rearrangement and greater phase instability.
Maximally homogeneous nanoparticles will undergo minimal compositional and phase changes after prolonged high-temperature exposure.
Maximally homogeneous nanoparticles will retain catalytic and thermoelectric performance after prolonged high-temperature exposure.
Deliberately inhomogeneous nanoparticles will exhibit greater elemental segregation, including noble-metal clustering.
Deliberately inhomogeneous nanoparticles will lose more catalytic performance than the one-pot baseline.
Conventional one-pot synthesis provides nanoparticles with initially uniform composition and satisfactory activity at moderate temperatures.
The proposed effect applies to near-equiatomic, multi-element systems whose constituent elements differ in atomic size and reduction potential.
Extreme initial compositional heterogeneity may eliminate the proposed stabilization effect.
Strong environmental oxidation may override the intrinsic kinetic barriers to segregation and phase transformation.
